title: Heavier than the earth
hook: Yudhishthira reads the shore, agrees to answer, and calls a mother heavier than the earth
carry: honor parents: heavier than earth, higher than sky

segments.voice: Yesterday: the yaksha, the unseen owner of the lake, and four brothers who took the water without asking. Your line was ask the earth's leave before you take.
screen: `THE YAKSHA'S QUESTIONS.` · `FOUR BROTHERS ON THE SHORE.`

segments.voice: The last brother comes alone. Yudhishthira has waited under the tree as long as he can, and now he follows the cranes himself. He finds the lake, and all four of his brothers lying beside it. He weeps over each of them by name, and remembers what each one was to him. And then, through his grief, he does something none of them did. He looks. Before he touches the water, he reads the shore.
screen: `THE LAST BROTHER COMES ALONE.` → `HE WEEPS OVER EACH ONE.` → `THEN HE LOOKS.`

segments.voice: What Yudhishthira sees doesn't add up. No wounds on his brothers. No footprints of an enemy. Their faces haven't changed color, so he doesn't think it's poison. He steps down into the water, and the voice comes. I am a crane, it says. I killed your brothers. Answer my questions, or you'll be the fifth. No bird could do this, Yudhishthira says. Who are you? And he sees a yaksha, a huge spirit, speaking from up in a tree. Yudhishthira doesn't shoot, or fight, or drink. I don't want what's yours, he says. Ask, and I'll answer as well as I'm able. The questions begin. What is heavier than the earth? A mother. What is higher than the sky? A father. What is faster than the wind? The mind. What is more numerous than blades of grass? Our thoughts. The yaksha asks about the size of the world, and Yudhishthira answers with a family. This is one of Hinduism's oldest teachings. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher sends his students home with these words: let your mother be a god to you, let your father be a god to you. It's why Hindu children bow and touch the feet of their parents and elders, and get a hand on the head and a blessing back. Not because elders are always right. Because what they carried for you weighs more than the earth.
screen: `NO WOUNDS, NO FOOTPRINTS.` · `I AM A CRANE. WHO ARE YOU?` · `HEAVIER THAN THE EARTH? A MOTHER.` · then, large: `LET YOUR MOTHER BE A GOD TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind your mother, your father, or whoever raised you, or an elder who has been good to you. Let their face come clear, and remember one thing they carried for you. If they're living, plan a pranam: touch their feet next time you see them, or call and ask their blessing. If they've died, or it's complicated, hold them as you can. If you pray, bring them into your prayer.
Yaksha-prashna, the yaksha's questions, which Yudhishthira is the first to answer. The brother who stops to look, offers to answer, and names a mother heavier than the earth. Today's word.
Your line: honor parents, heavier than earth, higher than sky. A mother, a father, a mind, a field of thoughts. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 803 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FOUR FRIENDS FOR FOUR SEASONS.`

howItsDone: In the epic, the yaksha's questions often sound like riddles, and Yudhishthira's first answers here point to mother and father; Hindu children honor parents and elders by touching their feet.

Yaksha-prashna.meaning: the yaksha's questions, the name of this episode

yaksha.meaning: a spirit; here, the unseen owner of the lake

Yudhishthira.meaning: eldest of the five Pandava brothers

pranam.meaning: a respectful bow; often touching an elder's feet

recall: a princess sent out to choose a husband

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), the episode of the Yaksha's questions: Yudhishthira at the lake; the crane and the yaksha; the first questions (heavier than the earth, higher than the sky, faster than the wind, more numerous than grass)
Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11 (the teacher's parting words: let your mother be a god to you, let your father be a god to you)
Touching the feet of parents and elders (pranam, charan sparsh), in general

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: Yudhishthira notes no wounds, no footprints, unchanged faces (ruling out poison); the voice first claims to be a crane; the yaksha's appearance beside a tree; Yudhishthira's reply that he does not covet what is the yaksha's.

Confirm the four answers: mother weightier than the earth, father higher than heaven, mind fleeter than wind, thoughts more numerous than grass. Other questions come earlier in the sequence in Ganguli; the script presents these as 'some of them'.
Original यक्षप्रश्न: confirm as the traditional name of the episode.

Editor pass: these four are not the first questions in Ganguli, so the hook no longer calls them 'the first'; 'this is how the whole contest will go' softened; the practice no longer gives the 'faster than the wind' answer to thoughts (the text gives it to the mind); garbled prayer line fixed; howItsDone no longer claims how the episode is 'often taught'.
